newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Holbrooke urges quick start to Holocaust payouts.
newsitem.headline: Holbrooke urges quick start to Holocaust payouts.

text.p: Influential American diplomat-cum-banker Richard Holbrooke urged Switzerland on Monday to start paying funds to Holocaust survivors at once to help resolve the "crisis" in U.S.-Swiss relations.

Defending a U.S. government report that criticised Swiss gold purchases from Nazi Germany during World War Two, Holbrooke urged Swiss officials not to get bogged down in a debate over historical details and instead to get money flowing to victims.

"It is vitally important to get the humanitarian fund that was initiated by the three big Swiss banks going right away," Holbrooke told the Swiss-American Chamber of Commerce, noting that the average age of the 400,000 Holocaust survivors was 79.

This 265-million Swiss franc ($185-million) memorial fund was set up amid boycott threats from foreign Jewish groups who accuse the banks of hoarding the dormant wealth that Jews murdered by the Nazis had stashed in Switzerland for safekeeping.
"We have to face the fact that this is not just another problem," said Holbrooke, a former U.S. assistant secretary of state.
"This is the most serious problem between our two countries at least since the end of the Second World War and perhaps in history....The fact is, it is a crisis."

After weeks of wrangling with Jewish groups, Berne in late May approved the memorial fund's executive board and advisory council. But no payments to needy Holocaust victims and their families have yet been made.

Struggling to handle allegations that the Swiss cynically profited from World War Two, Berne rejects charges in the U.S. study that its business deals with Germany prolonged the war and insists the neutral Swiss were not "bankers to the Nazis".

The report, compiled by U.S. Under-Secretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat, outraged many Swiss and stiffened opposition to the government's plan to sell part of Swiss gold reserves to finance a seven billion Swiss franc ($5 billion) humanitarian foundation.
Swiss voters must approve the plan next year in a referendum which is shaping up as a watershed in Swiss foreign and domestic policy.

"What is essential is to get these two funds going and to start the disbursement of funds as quickly as possible to the claimants," said Holbrooke, who is best known for brokering peace in former Yugoslavia.
"Delay only serves the purposes of those people in the United States and elsewhere...who wish to make this into something other than what it is."
Holbrooke, now vice-chairman of Credit Suisse First Boston bank, defended Eizenstat, his former aide, and insisted the U.S. government was not anti-Swiss.
"You may disagree with portions of Eizenstat's report, but an argument over the historical details is of no value to solve the problem," he said.
"He did the best he could. I think it is a fine report, without endorsing every word because I am not a historian."
Swiss officials have pledged to make a full accounting of the country's wartime past as a financial centre.
They relaxed banking secrecy to let an independent panel of historians review the era. A joint Swiss-Jewish group is also going through bank records to search for any missing wealth.
In Berne, the cabinet backed a proposal from parliament to protect any people who come forward and testify to the historical panel about their employers.
